payload.title: Fixing Things Again
paragraphs: On the first Saturday of every month, a hall in the north of the city fills with broken things. People arrive carrying lamps that no longer light, radios that hiss, and jackets with torn linings. Waiting for them are volunteers with screwdrivers, sewing machines and, above all, patience. Nothing is sold and nothing is thrown away; the only rule is that owners must sit beside their own object while it is repaired.

The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009 and has since spread to more than two thousand towns. Part of its appeal is financial, but the volunteers insist that saving money is not the main point. Most modern goods are designed to be replaced rather than opened, and glued cases and unlabelled parts make repair look impossible. A café shows, in an hour or two, that it often is not.

Measured in kilograms, the effect is modest: a busy session might save a few hundred items from landfill, a fraction of what one city discards in a day. Its organisers argue that the real product is confidence. Someone who has watched a kettle come apart on a table is slower to believe that a broken thing is finished, and that habit follows them home.

payload.title: The Wolves Came Back
paragraphs: When the last wolf in the region was shot in 1893, farmers celebrated. A century later, without anyone releasing them, wolves walked back across the border. They had followed river valleys and quiet motorway verges from populations further east, and the first proof was not a photograph but a line of prints in spring mud.

Ecologists welcomed the return, and not only for the sake of the animal itself. Deer numbers had grown so high that young trees were eaten before they could reach the height of a person, and the forest was slowly ageing without replacing itself. Where wolves now hunt, deer move more often and graze in shorter bursts, and thin lines of new saplings have appeared along the streams.

For the farmers whose sheep are killed, none of this is comforting. Compensation schemes pay for animals that are found, but not for the ones that simply vanish, and not for the work of bringing a flock in every night. The debate is therefore less about biology than about who carries the cost of a shared decision, and that is a harder problem to solve than any fence.
